input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

the final page of the catalogue is a short note from grandma rose about the photograph of the cousins beside the pear tree she wrote that the picture was made after the harvest supper and that everyone had gone back for a second piece of pie the note gives no year and the people in the picture are listed from left to right as ellen frank and a child whose name she could not remember that page should be scanned after the last numbered album page even though it has no number of its own the scan file can carry the label pear tree note and remain at the end of the folder so the uncertain child is not accidentally entered as a confirmed name", "output": "The family photo catalogue has been sitting on the dining room table since the first weekend in March, and we have finally agreed on one clear next step, which is forwarding the new scans to Aunt Lena before the reunion—not the whole catalogue, just the scans she asked for: the pictures of the north side of the family. The table is still needed for dinner, so I have been moving the folders into the blue crate each afternoon and putting the crate back beside the bookcase before anyone comes over. Nobody has changed the order of the original prints, and the handwritten labels are still facing up.

Grandma Rose began the catalogue in a green ledger in 1988, and Dad added dates in pencil whenever he knew them. The ledger lists the photographer or the person who donated a print, but it does not say that every date is certain. The picture of the three children by the apple shed is marked “about 1951,” and Uncle Peter thinks it may have been taken a year later because the shed roof was repaired in the summer of 1952. We should leave the wording as it is until someone finds a dated copy. The scan folder has a separate note for that question and does not replace the ledger.

Mara is checking the names with Aunt Lena over the phone, and she has kept a sheet of spellings beside the laptop. Lena said, “The envelope says, ‘Keep these dry,’” and she wants that sentence entered exactly because it is written under the flap of the brown paper sleeve. The sleeve holds six small prints from the lake picnic, and one of them has a faint crease across the corner. The crease is visible in the scan, but Mara has not tried to remove it, and she has not written a date on the back of any original. The family agreed last winter that uncertain names stay uncertain until somebody can point to a record or recognize the person.

The scanner is on the cabinet in the spare room, and the card with its settings is taped inside the top drawer. We are using the flat surface for loose prints and the paper guide for the longer album pages. Each scan is saved with the ledger number followed by a short subject name, so the files sort in the same order as the catalogue. The scan of the railway platform is numbered 44, and the scan of the garden party is numbered 45. There is also an unnumbered image of a small dog because nobody has found a matching entry yet. It stays in a temporary folder rather than being given a number that could belong to something else.

The inventory has six notes:
1. The tin box holds school portraits from the west family branch, and its lid has a dent near the hinge.
2. The album with the cloth cover has loose corners, but every page is still attached.
3. The two photographs in the glass frame should stay in the frame until Uncle Ray can bring the soft opening tool.
4. The envelope from the lake picnic is stored behind the ledger and not inside it.
5. The scan of the orchard group needs a second look because the lower edge is darker than the print.
6. The catalogue does not include postcards, so the card from Mill Bay belongs in the separate correspondence folder.

Last Thursday, Noah wrote that he could pick up the blue crate on Saturday morning if the rain held off, but the weather changed and nobody came to the house. The crate was not left outside, and I put it in the hall closet before the floor cleaner arrived. The small box of duplicate prints is on the top shelf of that closet and is not part of the scans for Lena. We should not mix those duplicates with the originals while packing because their paper is thinner, and the names on the duplicate envelopes were copied by hand years after the pictures were taken.

There is one condition that may change the timing: if the replacement sleeve arrives before Friday, then we can pack the lake picnic prints in it and include that sleeve with the scans. Otherwise, the loose prints stay in the current brown envelope until the next visit. The order for the scans does not depend on the sleeve, and the forwarding can still happen without sending any original material. Lena has asked to receive the files by email because her tablet cannot read the discs from the old computer. She also wants a plain list of the ledger numbers in the message so she can compare the files with the notes she has at home.

After the scans are forwarded, the blue crate can return to the shelf in the hall, and the ledger can go back into the drawer under the telephone table. Nobody has asked me to mail the original prints, and I have not promised to send them. The family can look at the scanned pictures during the reunion while the originals remain here. That arrangement matters because the old frames are fragile, and the brown sleeve is already soft at the fold. If Lena spots a name she recognizes, she can tell Mara which number to revisit, but no name is being added before she has checked her own albums.

The final page of the catalogue is a short note from Grandma Rose about the photograph of the cousins beside the pear tree. She wrote that the picture was made after the harvest supper and that everyone had gone back for a second piece of pie. The note gives no year, and the people in the picture are listed from left to right as Ellen, Frank, and a child whose name she could not remember. That page should be scanned after the last numbered album page, even though it has no number of its own. The scan file can carry the label “pear tree note” and remain at the end of the folder so the uncertain child is not accidentally entered as a confirmed name."}]
